resources.string: How club cells protect small airways

A qualitative look at club cells in a normal human bronchiole, from their shape to their secretions. The final chapter shows an example of local lining renewal and repair from mouse bronchioles, not an established sequence in humans. Shapes and timing are schematic.
Find a club cell in a small bronchiole
A cut across a small bronchiole shows the open airway and the thin layer of cells around it. Club cells sit among other cells in this layer, inside the smooth muscle of the airway wall.
Compare the dome with its neighbors
The apical surface, the side that faces the airway, bulges into a dome. It has no beating cilia, unlike neighboring ciliated cells. Dense secretory granules lie beneath the dome.

A granule moves toward the airway-facing surface and its membrane joins the cell membrane. The granule releases proteins, including club cell secretory protein (SCGB1A1), into the thin liquid lining the airway.
Proteins spread in the lining fluid
Once released, proteins such as SCGB1A1 spread within the liquid coating, rather than through the air. These secretions help protect the lining.
Renew a small patch of the lining

In mouse bronchioles, club cells can produce more club cells and new ciliated cells. This helps maintain and repair the lining locally. The animation shows one example, not a proven pathway in human bronchioles.
Evidence: club cell structure and secretory features in human small airways (Zuo et al.)
Evidence: bronchiolar lining maintenance and repair in mice (Rawlins et al.)
